newsitem.title: USA: Congressmen seek details on U.S. land swaps.
newsitem.headline: Congressmen seek details on U.S. land swaps.

text.p: The Clinton administration should give Congress details of its plans to protect a grove of ancient redwoods in California and land near Yellowstone National Park, two Republican congressmen said Thursday.

In a letter to President Clinton, House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston and the chairman of the interior appropriations subcommittee, Ralph Regula, said they were worried the administration was moving too quickly and without Congress' participation, setting a bad precedent.
Clinton has proposed swapping other federal assets for the endangered land.

"We worry that exchanges which sound positive at first glance, such as protecting old growth redwoods or stopping mining in Yellowstone National Park, are being implemented on a fast track which does not assure that the American public is getting full value for the traded Federal assets," Livingston of Louisiana and Regula of Ohio said.

But a White House spokesman denied there was a fast track for plans to compensate companies for halting a proposed massive gold mine outside Yellowstone and the cutting of redwoods in the Headwaters Grove in California, saying there would be a public airing of the plans.
There is a February 12 deadline for the administration to present options for the assets swaps for the proposed Crown Butte Resources Ltd's prospect outside of Yellowstone, the spokesman said.
He said those options will go through a public or congressional review, and said, "There certainly isn't any intention to do anything without public comment."
The congressmen's letter said settling the mine and redwood grove issues will involve trading more than $300 million in federal assets.
They said they were concerned that the administration "may be considering the transfer of Federal oil and gas resources without a thorough analysis of the full-life value of those energy resources."

"The administration may inadvertently establish a precedent for trading valuable Federal assets in the future," it said. "We urge you to seriously consider the downstream effects of such policy decisions."
